title: Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks — explain sequential append-only writes vs random I/O, zero-copy transfer (`sendfile`), and reliance on the OS page cache rather than an in-process cache.
shortTitle: Why can Kafka sustain very high throughput on commodity disks?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka achieves very high throughput on ordinary disks through three design choices. It stores each partition as an append-only log and writes sequentially, which is dramatically faster than random I/O even on spinning disks and still much faster on SSDs. It serves consumer reads with zero-copy transfer using the operating system's sendfile system call, which sends bytes straight from the page cache to the network socket without copying them through application memory. And it relies on the operating system page cache rather than maintaining its own in-process cache, so recent data is served from RAM for free and the JVM heap stays small, avoiding garbage-collection pressure.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India records every transaction in a long ledger. Instead of flipping around the ledger to find a spot for each entry, which is slow, clerks always write the next entry on the very next line at the end, which is fast and smooth; that is sequential append. When head office asks for a copy of recent pages, instead of a clerk photocopying each page by hand and walking it over, the bank uses a direct pass-through chute that sends the pages straight from the shelf to the courier without the clerk touching them; that is zero-copy. And because the most recent pages are already lying open on the desk from being written, anyone who wants them just reads them off the desk instead of fetching them from the vault; that is the operating-system page cache serving recent data from memory for free.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka is fast on cheap disks because it writes sequentially to an append-only log, serves reads with zero-copy sendfile straight from page cache to the socket, and leans on the OS page cache instead of an in-process cache, keeping the JVM heap small and avoiding garbage-collection stalls.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka achieves very high throughput on ordinary disks through three design choices. It stores each partition as an append-only log and writes sequentially, which is dramatically faster than random I/O even on spinning disks and still much faster on SSDs. It serves consumer reads with zero-copy transfer using the operating system's sendfile system call, which sends bytes straight from the page cache to the network socket without copying them through application memory. And it relies on the operating system page cache rather than maintaining its own in-process cache, so recent data is served from RAM for free and the JVM heap stays small, avoiding garbage-collection pressure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India records every transaction in a long ledger. Instead of flipping around the ledger to find a spot for each entry, which is slow, clerks always write the next entry on the very next line at the end, which is fast and smooth; that is sequential append. When head office asks for a copy of recent pages, instead of a clerk photocopying each page by hand and walking it over, the bank uses a direct pass-through chute that sends the pages straight from the shelf to the courier without the clerk touching them; that is zero-copy. And because the most recent pages are already lying open on the desk from being written, anyone who wants them just reads them off the desk instead of fetching them from the vault; that is the operating-system page cache serving recent data from memory for free.

**One line to remember:** Kafka is fast on cheap disks because it writes sequentially to an append-only log, serves reads with zero-copy sendfile straight from page cache to the socket, and leans on the OS page cache instead of an in-process cache, keeping the JVM heap small and avoiding garbage-collection stalls.

sections.s2_technical:
The first pillar is sequential append-only writes versus random I/O. A Kafka partition is an ordered log, and producers only ever append to the end of the active segment. Appending sequentially means the disk head, on a spinning disk, barely moves, and even on an SSD the controller can write large contiguous blocks efficiently with minimal write amplification. Random I/O, by contrast, scatters small writes all over the disk, forcing seeks on spinning disks and expensive read-modify-write cycles on SSDs. The performance gap between sequential and random access is enormous, often one to two orders of magnitude, which is why Kafka's append-only design lets commodity disks sustain throughput that would be impossible with a random-access data structure like a B-tree updated in place. Kafka also batches many records into one write and relies on the operating system to flush, so individual small producer records coalesce into large sequential disk writes.

The second pillar is zero-copy transfer with sendfile. When a consumer fetches records, those bytes often already sit in the operating system page cache because they were recently written or read. Without zero-copy, serving them would require copying the data from the kernel page cache into the application's user-space buffer, then back into the kernel socket buffer, then out to the network card, which is multiple copies and multiple context switches per transfer. Kafka instead uses the sendfile system call, which tells the kernel to transfer bytes directly from the page cache to the network socket without ever copying them into the JVM. In Java this is exposed through `FileChannel.transferTo`, and conceptually the hot path is:

```java
// Conceptually how Kafka serves a fetch: kernel moves bytes file -> socket directly.
fileChannel.transferTo(position, byteCount, socketChannel); // sendfile under the hood
// No copy into JVM heap, far fewer context switches, saturates the NIC.
```

This removes the per-byte cost of user-space copies, so a single broker can push data to many consumers at close to network line rate using very little CPU.

The third pillar is reliance on the operating-system page cache rather than an in-process cache. Many systems build their own large in-memory cache inside the application process. Kafka deliberately does not; it lets the operating system cache file data in the page cache, which is memory the OS already manages. This has several compounding benefits. Recently written data is already in the page cache, so consumers reading the tail of the log, which is the common case, are served from RAM without any disk read at all. Because the cache lives in the kernel and not the JVM heap, the Kafka process can run with a small heap, which keeps garbage-collection pauses short and predictable, a major reliability win since long GC pauses are a leading cause of broker instability. The page cache also survives a broker process restart, so a restarted broker can serve hot data from a warm cache immediately. And by not duplicating data in both an app cache and the OS cache, Kafka avoids wasting memory on double buffering.

These three pillars reinforce each other. Sequential writes keep recent data contiguous and hot in the page cache; the page cache makes most reads hit memory; and zero-copy then ships those cached bytes to consumers without touching the heap. The net effect is that the common path, producers appending and consumers reading the tail, involves almost no random disk access, almost no user-space copying, and almost no JVM memory pressure, which is exactly why Kafka saturates commodity hardware so well.

Senior-level nuances worth stating. Zero-copy is bypassed when the broker must transform bytes, for example when TLS encryption is enabled or when the broker must recompress or down-convert message formats for an older client, because those require the data to pass through user space, so you preserve the fast path by keeping client and broker message formats aligned and by being aware that encryption adds CPU and copies. Durability still depends on replication and flush behavior: Kafka relies on the page cache and the operating system to flush to disk lazily, trading an fsync-per-message for throughput, and it gets durability from replication across brokers rather than from forcing every write to disk immediately, which is why replication factor and acks settings, not disk fsync, are your durability contract. Finally, because Kafka leans on the page cache, you should give the operating system plenty of free RAM for caching rather than sizing a huge JVM heap, and you should expect performance to depend on how much of your working set fits in the page cache.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India streams card-authorization events through Kafka on commodity servers with ordinary SSDs, and the platform team was skeptical that cheap disks could handle the volume. Rajesh and Priya generate authorizations alongside millions of others.

Problem 1 — the team feared that writing millions of small authorization records per minute would thrash the disks with random I/O. In reality Kafka appends them sequentially to the partition log and batches them, so the disk sees large contiguous writes and keeps up easily. This is the sequential-write advantage.

Problem 2 — the team worried that fanning out those events to many consumer services would saturate broker CPU with data copying. In reality zero-copy sendfile ships bytes from the page cache straight to each consumer's socket, and the hot tail of the log is served from RAM via the page cache, so a single broker feeds many consumers cheaply. This is the zero-copy and page-cache advantage.

Our runnable demo models the cost of sequential versus random writes, counts the copies and context switches for a naive user-space read versus a zero-copy transfer, and models page-cache hit rates for tail reads versus old reads, reporting the throughput difference. The classes are `ThroughputDemo`, `WritePattern`, `TransferPath`, and `PageCache`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one million card-authorization records produced and then fanned out to several consumer services.

Step 1: Producers send many small authorization records. The Kafka client batches them by size and a short linger, so instead of a million tiny disk operations, the broker receives large batches and appends them sequentially to the end of the active segment. The disk sees big contiguous writes, which commodity SSDs handle at high throughput with minimal write amplification.

Step 2: Compared with a hypothetical random-write data structure, the sequential append is roughly one to two orders of magnitude cheaper, as the demo's cost model shows, which is why cheap disks keep up with the write rate that the team feared would thrash them.

Step 3: Consumer services fetch recent authorizations. Because those records were just written, they are still in the operating-system page cache, so the broker reads them from RAM, not disk. The hot tail of the log is served from memory for free.

Step 4: To send those cached bytes to each consumer, the broker uses zero-copy sendfile, transferring the bytes directly from the page cache to the network socket without copying them into the JVM heap. The naive path would make four copies and several context switches per transfer; zero-copy collapses that to effectively one transfer with minimal CPU, so one broker feeds many consumers near network line rate.

Step 5: Because the cache lives in the kernel rather than the JVM, Kafka runs with a small heap, keeping garbage-collection pauses short and the broker stable, and the page cache stays warm across restarts. The three pillars together mean the common path, appending and reading the tail, involves almost no random disk access, almost no user-space copying, and almost no heap pressure, which is the whole reason commodity hardware sustains such high throughput.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka sustains very high throughput on commodity disks because of three deliberate design choices that reinforce each other. The first is sequential append-only writes. A partition is an ordered log and producers only ever append to the end, so the disk sees large contiguous writes instead of scattered random ones. Sequential I/O is often one to two orders of magnitude faster than random I/O, on spinning disks because the head barely moves and on SSDs because it avoids expensive read-modify-write amplification, and Kafka batches many small records into big writes, so even millions of tiny events become efficient sequential appends that ordinary disks handle easily.

The second is zero-copy transfer using the sendfile system call. When a consumer fetches data, those bytes are usually already in the operating-system page cache, and rather than copying them from the kernel into the application's user-space buffer and back into the socket buffer, Kafka asks the kernel to transfer them directly from the page cache to the network socket. In Java this is FileChannel.transferTo, and it eliminates the per-byte user-space copies and most context switches, so a single broker can feed many consumers at close to network line rate using very little CPU.

The third is relying on the operating-system page cache instead of an in-process cache. Kafka does not build its own big heap cache; it lets the OS cache file data in memory it already manages. Because recently written data is already in the page cache, consumers reading the tail of the log, which is the common case, are served from RAM with no disk read at all. Because the cache lives in the kernel and not the JVM heap, Kafka runs with a small heap, which keeps garbage-collection pauses short and the broker stable, and the cache even survives a process restart so a restarted broker serves hot data immediately.

On the National Bank of India card-authorization stream, this is exactly why cheap servers with ordinary SSDs kept up with millions of events. The writes were sequential batched appends rather than random thrashing, the hot tail was served from the page cache, and zero-copy let one broker fan those events out to the fraud scorer, the ledger updater, and analytics without saturating CPU. The nuances I always mention are that zero-copy is bypassed when the broker must transform bytes, such as with TLS encryption or message-format down-conversion for old clients, so I keep client and broker formats aligned and budget CPU for encryption; that durability comes from replication and the acks contract rather than forcing an fsync per message, since Kafka flushes lazily through the page cache; and that because Kafka leans on the page cache, you give the operating system plenty of free RAM instead of sizing a giant heap. The one-line principle is that Kafka wins by turning messaging into sequential log appends and cached, zero-copy reads, which is the pattern commodity hardware is best at.
